data.title: Trump says he'll spend 'a lot' of MAGA Inc. war chest in midterms
data.description:
President Trump said he’s prepared to spend ‘a lot’ of money from his MAGA Inc. war chest to support Republican candidates in this midterm cycle.

“Well, I’ve raised a lot, and nobody knows what it is, but I will tell you it’s about $850 million,” Trump said before boarding Air Force One to fly to South Carolina. “I’ll be spending a lot of that money for — and my own money, but I’ll be spending a lot of that money for candidates that I think are good, Republican candidates.”

“We’re in very good shape,” he added.

Election forecasters favor Democrats to win the House and give Republicans a slight edge in the Senate race, though momentum is moving against the GOP, due largely to Trump’s sinking approval and the Iran war.

MAGA Inc. is a super PAC that heavily supported Trump’s 2024 campaign.

Trump said earlier this month in an interview with Punchbowl News that he could “spend it on pretty much anything I want.”

“I’m going to help Republicans,” he said.

So far, the super PAC hasn’t spent any money on candidates in June or July.

Some Republicans told Politico last month that they wish the president would start opening up the coffers to help GOP candidates.

James Blair, a top Trump political adviser who oversees the super PAC, said the president “is going to expend substantial resources to win the midterms.”

“He cares deeply about the party winning and anything he can do to support that he is going to do and is already doing,” Blair said on “The Sean Spicer Show” in June.

He wouldn’t say when the money would be sent, only saying it would be “very soon.”

data.title: Watch live: Trump stumps for Darline Graham in South Carolina
data.description:
President Trump will hit the campaign trail in South Carolina Friday to rally support for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) ahead of the state’s Republican runoff next week, where she’s set to face off against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.).

Trump’s appearance comes as Graham faces scrutiny for a rough debate performance earlier this week, after which she was slammed over her lack of knowledge on national security issues.

Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), was appointed last month by GOP Gov. Henry McMaster to fill out the remainder of her brother’s term. The political newcomer is relying heavily on the president’s endorsement to keep her seat in the upper chamber.

Prominent Palmetto State Republicans, many of whom also vied for the spot, are split between Graham and Norman. Rep. Russell Fry, who finished third in the initial primary, has backed the incumbent, while former Gov. Mark Sanford (R) has endorsed her challenger. The campaign stop will be in Myrtle Beach, S.C., which falls in Fry’s 7th Congressional District.

The event is scheduled to begin at 7 p.m. EDT.

Watch the live video above.

data.title: Trump has mountain of Leavitt replacements, says Scott Jennings 'is good'
data.description:
President Trump on Friday said he’s never seen so many job applications in his life in response to the opening created by Karoline Leavitt’s decision to leave her post as White House press secretary.

Asked by reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland about who he was considering to replace Leavitt, Trump declined to give a name but signaled the choice could be difficult.

Pointing to different reporters standing on the tarmac with him, Trump said, “I don’t know, maybe you.”

“I will tell you this, and Karoline will tell you this, I have never seen so many job applications in my life,” he added.

Leavitt, who was standing next to Trump, nodded in agreement, agreed “there’s a lot of options.”

The president continued that Leavitt “made that job very glamorous” so “they all want that job; they love that job.”

A reporter asked him during the gaggle about whether CNN political commentator Scott Jennings was being considered for the position.

“Scott Jennings is good,” the president responded.

Jennings has worked on two campaigns for former President George W. Bush and served as an adviser to Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), and been CNN’s primary conservative analyst since 2017. He was reportedly being considered for the position in 2024 following Trump’s election win. 

In an Aug. 13 appearance on “CNN News Night,” Jennings told other panelists that he did not know if he would replace Leavitt.

“But I’ll tell you this: Karoline Leavitt has been maybe the greatest White House press secretary in the last 30 years, at least. She’s been nothing short of brilliant,” he stated. “I don’t know a single Republican in the country who isn’t in awe of and in appreciation of Karoline tonight.”

Leavitt said she was leaving the job to care for his two young children.

“I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary,” she said earlier this month.

She has been Trump’s only press secretary in his second term. During Trump’s first term, Sean Spicer, now-Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R), Stephanie Grisham and Kayleigh McEnany served in the role.

data.title: Pentagon fires Stars and Stripes editor-in-chief, publisher, reporter
data.description:
The Pentagon fired the publisher, editor-in-chief and at least one reporter at Stars and Stripes, a historically independent military news outlet, on Friday as the department has looked to reshape its coverage in recent months. 

The Defense Department (DOD) dismissed Erik Slavin, the editor-in-chief, publisher Max Lederer and Middle East correspondent Lara Korte, Star and Stripes reported on Friday. 

Slavin said he was ousted for insubordination after telling CBS News in an interview that potential censorship of news for U.S. service members would be a red line,

Korte confirmed her firing on social media, saying it was for “insubordination after I told a CBS reporter that I work for Stars and Stripes – not the Pentagon, not any administration, and not any policy maker.” 

“I consider it a great privilege to live alongside members of the military and share their stories. It’s a shame for the institution and service members, who swore to defend the Constitution and deserve the right to a free and independent press,” Korte said on social platform X. 

Stars and Stripes has traditionally enjoyed independence from DOD, even though its staff are Pentagon employees and it’s partially funded by the department. 

Earlier this week, Lederer said he would retire from his role by Sept. 30, since his “understanding of the value and mission” of the outlet is different in “fundamental ways” from the plans DOD has for the newspaper. 

“I have thought a great deal about the right time to step aside, and I have concluded that this is it,” Lederer said in a note to staff. “I leave with real pride in what we have accomplished together and with complete confidence in what you will accomplish next.”

DOD installed Navy Capt. William Urban, an active duty service member, as the new deputy publisher a few weeks ago, prompting questions from three Democratic senators. 

Journalism groups slammed the Pentagon for ousting Slavin, arguing it is another attempt by the department to dictate news coverage of the outlet. 

“This is an assault on the fundamental principle that journalists must be free to report the news without fear of retaliation from the government officials they cover,” the National Press Club President Mark Schoeff Jr. said in a statement on Friday. “The Pentagon must reaffirm that principle and make clear that Stars and Stripes journalists will not be punished for doing their jobs.” 

The Pentagon has sought to refocus coverage on “warfighting” and remove what it calls “woke distractions” in the outlet’s coverage.

“We will modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members,” Pentagon Chief spokesperson Sean Parnell said in January. 

In April, DOD removed the newspaper’s ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith, the person in charge of monitoring the outlet’s editorial independence and reporting concerns to Congress. 

“Apparently the Pentagon also doesn’t want you to hear from me anymore about threats to the editorial independence of Stars and Stripes,” Smith wrote in an op-ed for The Wall Street Journal at the time.

data.title: Trump defends beef import plan after GOP blowback
data.description:
President Trump Friday defended his decision to temporary suspend higher tariffs on ground beef imports, saying it’s “what the people want.”

“We want to get the beef prices down so we will get them down a little bit,” Trump said before boarding Air Force One to fly to South Carolina.  “That’s what people want, that’s what the voters want, and that’s what I want.”

“The ranchers are great. They are my people. I love the ranchers; they’ve done a fantastic job,” he added. “But they admit that we need a little help in order to get the prices down, so that is what we’re doing.”

Trump in a social media post earlier Friday announced that he was temporarily lifting certain tariffs on imported ground beef to lower the cost of beef for consumers. The suspension would be for 90 days and would allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported.

He also said a deal was coming that would lower the price of ground beef to 25 percent below the current market price but didn’t say where the beef would be coming from.

When asked at Joint Base Andrews what countries the deal was with, he said he didn’t want to say.

“There are a few countries but they’re going to be sending in the highest quality beef and it’s something that we need,” he said.

Ranchers and GOP lawmakers immediately criticized the president’s announcement.

Colin Woodall, CEO of the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association, said in a statement that the association was “disappointed” by the decision.

“While America’s cattle producers share the goal of keeping groceries affordable for consumers, flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd,”  Woodall said. “Cattle markets have already turned sharply lower this morning, to the detriment of farmers and ranchers.”

“This is a critical time of year for cattle producers, as we approach the season where they are making decisions regarding their herds,” he added. “Cattle farmers and ranchers are responding to strong market signals and historically high demand, and we are already working to rebuild after years of ongoing drought, high input costs and other challenges that have reduced U.S. cattle numbers.”

He said the announcement throws “cold water” on the idea of expanding herds.

Meriwether Farms, a farm-to-table cattle operation from Wyoming, called the president’s actions a “betrayal” on social media.

Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) said she was “extremely disappointed” with the decision.

“We all want lower grocery prices, but as I’ve said for months, we cannot do it at the expense of American producers,” she wrote on X. “Flooding the market with foreign beef hurts our livestock industry and undermines the long-term solution: growing the U.S. cattle herd to meet demand.”

data.title: Live updates: Trump lifts beef import tariffs, heads to South Carolina to rally for Graham
data.description:
President Trump on Friday sought to ease price pressure on beef prices by temporarily lifting the tariffs on imported beef. The move drew swift and sharp rebukes from some lawmakers and ranchers.

Trump is set to hit the campaign trail Friday in an attempt to give Republican Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.) one last boost before the special GOP primary runoff Tuesday.

Graham, a political newcomer who replaced her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), is going up against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) for the opportunity to snag the Republican seat in the Palmetto State.

Darline Graham’s inexperience showed on the debate stage Tuesday when she was unable to answer a national security question, raising uncertainty about her ability to serve in the Senate.

The Supreme Court on Friday temporarily halted an appeals court order that would’ve stopped above-ground construction on the White House ballroom. Chief Justice John Roberts’s administrative stay gives the court additional time to consider the administration’s emergency appeal but contains no explanation. It does not necessarily reflect the court’s thinking on the underlying legal issues.

IndyCar will take over the District of Columbia this weekend, with the Freedom 250 race Saturday and Sunday. It may cause a “little bit of carnage,” the IndyCar chief said.

Follow live below.

data.title: Interior shuffles several senior career staffers
data.description:
The Interior Department has recently shuffled at least 25 senior career staffers, giving them different roles at the department that oversees that nation’s public lands, parks and other resources, a source familiar told The Hill. 

The employees who were shuffled to new positions at the department belong to the senior executive service (SES), a group of highly experienced upper-level officials who are career staffers rather than political appointees. 

The specific reasons for the shuffle are not entirely clear. Reached for comment, an Interior Department spokesperson said that while it does not comment on individual personnel matters,  “SES reassignments are a routine management tool used across administrations.”

“The Department continues to align senior leadership and resources to best support its mission, improve organizational effectiveness and deliver results for the American people,” said the spokesperson, who did not sign their name to the email. 

The Trump administration has repeatedly sought to make changes to the federal workforce — and in particular has sought to downsize it.

Last fall, Interior considered cutting hundreds of jobs, though the widespread cuts it floated at the time did not appear to come to fruition.

data.title: Appeals court slashes Alex Jones Sandy Hook judgment from $50M to $1.5M
data.description:
A Texas court on Friday cut the amount Infowars founder Alex Jones was ordered to pay to a family affected by the Sandy Hook shooting after they were subject to harassment when he claimed the attack was a hoax.

The Third Court of Appeals ruled unanimously to reduce the damages awarded to Neil Heslin and Scarlett Lewis from more than $45 million to $1.5 million, according to court documents. 

“The Court modifies the trial court’s judgment by reducing the exemplary damages award consistent with the statutory cap, resulting in exemplary damages awards of $750,000 to Scarlett Lewis and of $750,000 to Neil Heslin,” Chief Justice of the Third Court of Appeals of Texas Darlene Bryne wrote in her opinion Friday.

It found that there was no evidence that showed the harassment the couple endured from the claims Jones made allowed for the cap to be exceeded.

The ruling did not touch the $4.1 million Jones owes in compensatory damages to Heslin and Lewis, who lost their 6-year-old son in the shooting. Their son was among 20 children and six educators killed in the 2012 attack in Newtown, Connecticut.

On Friday, Jones said his legal team will continue to appeal the case to the state Supreme Court to get the remaining damages thrown out.

This ruling also does not affect the $1.25 billion Jones still has to pay to other families in Connecticut after he was found to be liable for harassment they endured when he claimed the mass shooting never happened. 

The Supreme Court in 2025 turned down Jones’s petition to avoid paying the sum which had plunged him into bankruptcy. 

Jones has yet to make any payments in either state as he continues to appeal the damage amounts and the attempt to liquidate his company, Free Speech Systems (FSS), which oversees Infowars. 

The Texas court in May had paused efforts made by satirical outlet The Onion from taking over FSS and Infowars. The deal would have given the outlet temporary authority and use of its trademarks. 

Jones has fought to retain control over the company and called the deal “illegal.”

data.title: Outbreak linked to alfalfa sprouts; people sickened with E. coli and Salmonella
data.description:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said Friday that alfalfa sprouts are linked to a current E. coli and salmonella outbreak.

The agency has tied several food-borne illness cases to the consumption of alfalfa sold under the Calco and Everything Sprouts brands, also urging Americans who have purchased the affected sprouts to throw them away or return them.

The contaminated alfalfa sprouts have sparked the third ongoing salmonella outbreak this month and second E. coli ongoing outbreak since the beginning of the year. In late July, the agency identified certain shelled eggs as a source of salmonella and later recalled some frozen blueberries for posing a severe risk of E. coli infection.

As of Friday, the CDC reported that the 55 reported cases were spread across 14 states, four of which resulted in hospitalization. While interviewing infected individuals, 76% had reported eating the sprout in the week before they got sick.

Most people impacted by the outbreak only contracted one of the illnesses — with 46 contracting E. coli and seven Salmonella. The remaining two caught both.

But the CDC estimates the number could be higher, as its common for those infected with salmonella and E. coli to recover without receiving medical care. 

The CDC believes to the outbreak began between May 31 and Aug. 8, and traceback data tied infections to alfalfa from Calco and Everything Sprouts — both sold at grocery stores and restaurants.

Cases in Minnesota and Wisconsin accounted for nearly 70 percent of recorded infections. The CDC traced back some of these cases to restaurants in both states that reported using Everything Sprouts-branded alfalfa.

Officials are still continuing to investigate this outbreak, which involves three different strains of E. coli and one strain of salmonella.

Salmonella is a common foodborne illness causing diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps. The CDC estimates that these symptoms can emerge between six hours and six days after infection and last four to seven days. 

Common symptoms of an E. coli infection are similar to salmonella but can also include stomach cramps, bloody stool or urine, vomiting and dehydration, according to the Food and Drug Administration. They can begin just a few days to as much as nine days after ingesting E. coli bacteria.

Investigators found the percentage of infected individuals who ate alfalfa was much higher than the number of Americans who report eating it, supporting their finding that the sprout caused the illness.

The CDC’s FoodNet Population survey — used to estimate how often Americans eat foods commonly linked to illness — found only 8.7 percent of respondents had eaten the sprout within the past seven days.

data.title: Reports of sexual assault in military dropped for third year in a row: Pentagon
data.description:
Reports of sexual assault in the U.S. military dropped for the third year in a row in 2025, and the Pentagon received a slightly lower number of sexual harassment complaints last year compared to 2024, the department said in a new report that was made public on Friday. 

The Pentagon received a total of 7,998 reports of sexual assault in 2025, down from the previous year’s 8,195 reports. There were 8,515 reports of sexual assault in 2023 and 8,942 reports in 2022. 

Out of the 7,998 reports in 2025, 5,022 were unrestricted reports and 2,976 remained restricted at the end of Fiscal Year 2025, the Pentagon said in the 29-page report. 

Unrestricted reports for sexual harassment or sexual assault are reported to the chain of command and it results in an official probe, allowing service members to access mental health care and legal assistance. 

“Dignity, respect and discipline are foundational to the warrior ethos and the overall preparedness of the force. Sexual assault and sexual harassment undermine these values, eroding trust and threatening the mission,” Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony J. Tata said in a statement. 

“The FY 2025 report underscores our ongoing commitment to maintaining high standards, protecting our people, and building a unified, ready and lethal fighting force,” Tata said.

During 2025, the Pentagon received 2,936 sexual harassment complaints, a bit lower than in 2024 when the department got 3,014 complaints. 

The Pentagon is obligated to send an annual report to Congress as outlined in Section 1631 of the 2011 Ike Skelton National Defense Authorization Act. The 2025 report was delivered to the Senate and House Armed Services Committees, along with the House and Senate Veterans Affairs panels on Aug. 10. 

The Marine Corps had the highest percentage of women experiencing unwanted sexual contact among service branches with 6.4 percent, followed by 5.1 percent in the Navy and 4.5 percent in the Army. The Air Force was the lowest at 2.8 percent. 

Among men, the Navy was the highest at 1.5 percent in 2025. Army and Marine Corps were at 1 percent, the report said. 

The Pentagon said the estimated rate of unwanted sexual contact for active-duty women fell from 6.8 percent in 2023 to 4.3 percent in 2025. A third of victims came forward last year, an increase from a quarter in 2023. 

“This statistically significant decrease in estimated prevalence was mostly driven by fewer enlisted women (E1-E4 and E5-E9) and junior officer women (O1-O3) as well as women ages 35 and younger indicating past-year unwanted sexual contact on the survey,” the department wrote in the report. 

About 1 percent of active duty men indicated experiencing unwanted sexual contact in 2025, a slight decrease from 2023 when it was at 1.3 percent. 

Around 20,492 active service members, 9,860 active duty women and 10,632 active duty men, experienced unwanted sexual contact last year, a drop from 2023 when 29,061 active duty said the same. 

Outside groups pointed to the 2025 figure being nearly 40 percent higher than in 2016, when it was 14,900 and last year’s numbers being roughly identical to 2018, with 20,500. 

About a third of service members who indicated experiencing unwanted sexual contact last year reported their incident to their authority, an increase from 25 percent in 2023. 

The Pentagon had “sufficient” evidence to take disciplinary action in 1,321 cases of individuals probed for an allegation of sexual assault, the department said in the report. 

Josh Connolly, the senior vice president of Protect Our Defenders, a nonprofit group that works to end sexual misconduct in the military, said he would not take the Pentagon’s figures at “face value” and neither should the public. 

“Survivors are more afraid to come forward than they were two years ago, and this administration has spent the past year giving them reason to be – rolling back whistleblower protections, making it harder to report anonymously, warning people who come forward that they may be punished for it,” Connolly said in a statement on Friday. “A number that falls because people stopped talking is not progress.” 

Early last year, the Navy halted sexual assault prevention and response training. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in October last year that he would revamp offices with the Pentagon’s inspector general office and the department’s equal employment opportunity office that allowed service members to anonymously file whistleblower complaints. 

“Talk to those who do report,” Connolly said on Friday. “The vast majority of those cases go nowhere. Documents get lost. Evidence never gets used. They’re handed from one lawyer to the next, or never get one at all. Then they’re pushed out and lose their medical and mental health care on the way.”
